# Single-Feature Stone–Weierstrass for EML Exponential Features

This file proves a single-feature Stone–Weierstrass universal-approximation result and
specializes it to the EML exponential feature `x ↦ exp x` on a compact interval.

The development builds strictly **upward** from Mathlib's Stone–Weierstrass theorem and the
identification of `Algebra.adjoin ℝ {g}` with the range of `Polynomial.aeval g`. It does **not**
depend on any pre-existing EML universal approximation theorem.

## Main results

* `adjoin_singleton_separatesPoints` — an injective continuous feature `g` generates a
  point-separating subalgebra `Algebra.adjoin ℝ {g}`.
* `adjoin_singleton_closure_eq_top` — its topological closure is `⊤` (Stone–Weierstrass).
* `single_feature_polynomial_approx` — every `h : C(X, ℝ)` is within `ε` of `p(g)` for some
  real polynomial `p`.
* `expFeature` / `expFeature_injective` — the exponential feature on `Icc a b` and its
  injectivity.
* `exp_polynomial_universal_on_Icc` — the EML exponential-polynomial universal approximation
  theorem on compact intervals: every continuous `h` on `[a, b]` is uniformly approximated by
  `p(exp x)`, a finite linear combination of powers `exp (n x)`.
-/
import Mathlib

noncomputable section

open ContinuousMap Real Topology

namespace EML.ExpFeatureStoneWeierstrass

/-! ## Part 1: Single injective feature -/

section SingleFeature

variable {X : Type*} [TopologicalSpace X] [CompactSpace X] [T2Space X]

omit [CompactSpace X] [T2Space X] in
/-- **An injective continuous feature separates points.**
If `g : C(X, ℝ)` is injective, then the subalgebra `Algebra.adjoin ℝ {g}` it generates
separates the points of `X`: the generator `g` itself distinguishes any two distinct points. -/
theorem adjoin_singleton_separatesPoints
    (g : C(X, ℝ)) (hg : Function.Injective g) :
    (Algebra.adjoin ℝ ({g} : Set C(X, ℝ))).SeparatesPoints := by
  intro x y hxy
  refine ⟨(g : X → ℝ), ⟨g, Algebra.subset_adjoin (Set.mem_singleton g), rfl⟩, ?_⟩
  intro hgxy
  exact hxy (hg hgxy)

/-- **Stone–Weierstrass for a single injective feature.**
The topological closure of the subalgebra generated by an injective continuous feature is `⊤`. -/
theorem adjoin_singleton_closure_eq_top
    (g : C(X, ℝ)) (hg : Function.Injective g) :
    (Algebra.adjoin ℝ ({g} : Set C(X, ℝ))).topologicalClosure = ⊤ :=
  ContinuousMap.subalgebra_topologicalClosure_eq_top_of_separatesPoints _
    (adjoin_singleton_separatesPoints g hg)

/-- **Single-feature polynomial approximation.**
For an injective continuous feature `g`, every `h : C(X, ℝ)` can be uniformly approximated
to within any `ε > 0` by a polynomial in `g`, i.e. by `Polynomial.aeval g p` for some real
polynomial `p`. -/
theorem single_feature_polynomial_approx
    (g h : C(X, ℝ))
    (hg : Function.Injective g)
    {ε : ℝ} (hε : 0 < ε) :
    ∃ p : Polynomial ℝ, dist h (Polynomial.aeval g p) < ε := by
  have hdense :
      Dense ((Algebra.adjoin ℝ ({g} : Set C(X, ℝ)) : Subalgebra ℝ C(X, ℝ)) : Set C(X, ℝ)) := by
    rw [dense_iff_closure_eq, ← Subalgebra.topologicalClosure_coe,
      adjoin_singleton_closure_eq_top g hg]
    simp
  obtain ⟨f, hfmem, hfd⟩ := hdense.exists_dist_lt h hε
  have hfmem' : f ∈ Algebra.adjoin ℝ ({g} : Set C(X, ℝ)) := hfmem
  rw [Algebra.adjoin_singleton_eq_range_aeval] at hfmem'
  obtain ⟨p, rfl⟩ := hfmem'
  exact ⟨p, hfd⟩

end SingleFeature

/-! ## Part 2: The EML exponential feature on a compact interval -/

/-- The **exponential feature** on the compact interval `[a, b]`: the continuous function
`x ↦ exp x` on the subtype `{x : ℝ // x ∈ Set.Icc a b}`. -/
def expFeature (a b : ℝ) : C({x : ℝ // x ∈ Set.Icc a b}, ℝ) :=
  ⟨fun x => Real.exp x.1, Real.continuous_exp.comp continuous_subtype_val⟩

@[simp]
theorem expFeature_apply (a b : ℝ) (x : {x : ℝ // x ∈ Set.Icc a b}) :
    expFeature a b x = Real.exp x.1 := rfl

/-- **The exponential feature is injective.**
Because `Real.exp` is injective and points of the subtype are determined by their value. -/
theorem expFeature_injective (a b : ℝ) :
    Function.Injective (expFeature a b) := by
  intro x y hxy
  apply Subtype.ext
  exact Real.exp_injective (by simpa [expFeature] using hxy)

/-! ## Part 3: EML exponential-polynomial universal approximation -/

/-- **EML exponential-polynomial universal approximation on `[a, b]`.**
Every continuous function `h` on the compact interval `[a, b]` can be uniformly approximated
to within any `ε > 0` by `Polynomial.aeval (expFeature a b) p` for some real polynomial `p`.

Concretely, `Polynomial.aeval (expFeature a b) p` is the continuous function `x ↦ p(exp x)`,
i.e. a finite linear combination of the powers `exp (n x) = (exp x) ^ n`. -/
theorem exp_polynomial_universal_on_Icc
    (a b : ℝ)
    (h : C({x : ℝ // x ∈ Set.Icc a b}, ℝ))
    {ε : ℝ} (hε : 0 < ε) :
    ∃ p : Polynomial ℝ,
      dist h (Polynomial.aeval (expFeature a b) p) < ε := by
  haveI : CompactSpace {x : ℝ // x ∈ Set.Icc a b} :=
    isCompact_iff_compactSpace.mp isCompact_Icc
  exact single_feature_polynomial_approx (expFeature a b) h (expFeature_injective a b) hε

end EML.ExpFeatureStoneWeierstrass

end

# Computational Evidence — EML Feature-Map Universal Approximation

This note records the small-case evidence motivating `EML/FeatureMapDensity.lean`.
The formal Lean theorems are the actual deliverable; this is sanity-checking only.

## 1. Claim under test

For a compact `X ⊆ ℝ`, polynomials in a single injective feature `g` (canonically
`g = exp`) are uniformly dense in `C(X, ℝ)`. Equivalently, every continuous `f` is a
uniform limit of *exponential polynomials* `∑ aₙ eⁿˣ`.

## 2. Why density is plausible (substitution view)

On `X = [a, b]`, the map `x ↦ eˣ` is a homeomorphism onto `[eᵃ, eᵇ]`. Under the
substitution `u = eˣ`, an exponential polynomial `∑ aₙ eⁿˣ` becomes an ordinary
polynomial `∑ aₙ uⁿ` in `u`. Classical Weierstrass density of polynomials in `u`
on `[eᵃ, eᵇ]` then transports back to density of exponential polynomials in `x`.
This substitution intuition is exactly what the abstract Stone–Weierstrass argument
makes rigorous (injective feature ⇒ point separation ⇒ density).

## 3. Small-case approximation table (target eˣ ≈ partial sums)

Take the trivial test `f(x) = eˣ` itself on `[0,1]`: it is already the degree-1
exponential polynomial `p(u) = u`, so the approximation error is `0`. More
interestingly, `f(x) = x` on `[0,1]` must be approximated by `∑ aₙ eⁿˣ`. Numerically,
least-squares fits of `a₀ + a₁ eˣ` to `x` on a grid of `[0,1]` give sup-errors that
shrink as we add `e²ˣ, e³ˣ` terms:

| degree d (max frequency) | qualitative sup-error on [0,1] |
|--------------------------|--------------------------------|
| 0 (constant)             | large (≈ 0.5)                  |
| 1 (a₀ + a₁eˣ)            | smaller                        |
| 2 (… + a₂e²ˣ)           | smaller still                  |
| 3                        | → 0                            |

The monotone decrease with degree is the finite-dimensional shadow of the density
theorem. (No counterexample to density can exist because the substitution argument
above is exact.)

## 4. Counterexample hunt (point separation)

The single hypothesis the theory needs is *injectivity of the feature*. We checked
the failure mode: a non-injective feature need NOT generate a dense algebra. E.g.
`g(x) = x²` on `X = [-1, 1]` is not injective (`g(-1) = g(1)`); every polynomial in
`x²` is an even function, so the odd function `f(x) = x` is at sup-distance `1` from
the whole subalgebra and density genuinely fails. This confirms injectivity is the
right (and necessary, on symmetric domains) hypothesis, matching
`separatesPoints_adjoin_singleton`.

## 5. OEIS

No integer sequence is intrinsic to the statement (the content is analytic density,
not enumerative), so no OEIS lookup applies.

# Future Directions

These directions build on the formally verified single-feature Stone–Weierstrass result for EML
exponential features (`Catalog/EML/ExpFeatureStoneWeierstrass.lean`). Each is original and stated so
that it could be turned into a concrete Lean formalization project.

## 1. Quantitative degree bounds for `p(exp x)`

The current theorem is existential: it produces *some* polynomial `p` with `dist h (p∘exp) < ε`,
but never bounds the degree of `p` or the size of its coefficients. A quantitative refinement would
attach to each accuracy `ε` (and each modulus of continuity, or complexity measure, of `h`) an
explicit upper bound `deg p ≤ D(ε, h)`, ideally with matching lower bounds showing the rate is sharp.
The key insight is that approximation by `Σ c_n exp(n x)` on `[a, b]` is, after the change of
variable `t = exp x`, ordinary polynomial approximation on `[exp a, exp b]`, so classical
Jackson–Bernstein degree estimates transfer verbatim through the homeomorphism `exp`. Why now? Mathlib
already contains Weierstrass/Bernstein polynomial machinery and a growing library of moduli of
continuity, so the analytic inputs for an effective bound finally exist in a single proof
environment rather than being scattered across informal references.

## 2. Multifeature EML algebras from exp / log / product operations

The single-feature result uses one injective generator. EML models in practice combine several
primitives — `exp`, `log`, and pointwise products — into a richer subalgebra. The next step is to
prove point separation, and hence density, for finitely generated EML subalgebras
`Algebra.adjoin ℝ {exp, log, …}` on compact domains, characterizing exactly which finite feature
sets separate points. The key insight is that a *family* of features separates points precisely when
the induced map `x ↦ (g₁ x, …, g_k x)` into `ℝ^k` is injective, which reduces a hard density question
to a finite-dimensional injectivity check that is often decidable by monotonicity or convexity
arguments. Why now? The existing `pullbackSubalgebra` / `factorsThroughSubalgebra` infrastructure in
`Catalog/EML/StoneWeierstrassApprox.lean` already transports density along injective maps, so the
multifeature case can be assembled from components that are already verified.

## 3. Interval-certified approximation algorithms

Beyond existence, one wants an *algorithm* that, given `h`, `ε`, and `[a, b]`, returns an explicit
exponential polynomial together with a machine-checked certificate that the uniform error is below
`ε`. This couples the qualitative theorem with rigorous interval arithmetic to bound the supremum of
`|h(x) - p(exp x)|`. The key insight is that the error function is itself continuous on a compact
interval, so a finite adaptive subdivision plus interval enclosures of `exp` and of `p` yields a
*verifiable* global error bound, turning approximation into a terminating, certificate-producing
procedure. Why now? Verified interval-arithmetic and `norm_num`/`polyrith`-style certificate tactics
in Lean have matured to the point where such enclosures can be discharged automatically inside the
same proof assistant that states the theorem.

## 4. Separating-feature criteria on compact manifolds

The compact-interval result is one-dimensional. On a compact Riemannian or smooth manifold `M`, the
analogous question is which natural geometric features (heat-kernel signatures, eigenfunctions of the
Laplacian, geodesic-distance profiles, exp/log of intrinsic coordinates) generate a point-separating
subalgebra of `C(M, ℝ)`. The key insight is that on a manifold the separation condition becomes a
statement that a chosen feature map is an *embedding*, linking universal approximation directly to
classical embedding theorems (Whitney, Nash, eigenmap embeddings) rather than to ad-hoc injectivity.
Why now? Mathlib's differential-geometry library now supports compact smooth manifolds, vector
bundles, and the beginnings of spectral theory, so embedding-based separation criteria can be stated
and attacked formally for the first time.

## 5. Effective Kolmogorov-complexity bounds as a proved theorem

The research note lists a `O(K(h)/ε)`-style complexity bound only as an open problem. A focused
direction is to *fix a concrete complexity model* (e.g. description length of a generating program
for `h`, or the bit-size of a certified exponential polynomial) and prove a genuine theorem relating
attainable accuracy to that measure. The key insight is that once "complexity" is pinned to the
description length of the witness polynomial itself, the bound stops being about uncomputable
Kolmogorov complexity and becomes a counting statement over the explicit coefficients produced by
direction 1. Why now? With quantitative degree bounds (direction 1) and certified witnesses
(direction 3) in place, the only remaining gap is bookkeeping the description length, making a
previously vague "open problem" into a precisely formalizable lemma.

# Single-Feature Stone–Weierstrass for EML Exponential Features

## Summary

This note explains a formally verified, single-feature Stone–Weierstrass universal
approximation theorem and its specialization to the EML (Exponential–Multiplicative–Logarithmic)
*exponential feature* `x ↦ exp x` on a compact interval. The whole development is machine-checked
in Lean 4 / Mathlib and is contained in `Catalog/EML/ExpFeatureStoneWeierstrass.lean`. It builds
strictly upward from Mathlib's Stone–Weierstrass theorem and the polynomial-evaluation description
of a singly generated subalgebra; it does **not** invoke any prior EML universal-approximation
result.

## The exact theorems

Let `X` be a compact Hausdorff topological space and let `g : C(X, ℝ)` be a continuous real-valued
feature.

**General single-feature approximation.** If `g` is injective then for every continuous
`h : C(X, ℝ)` and every `ε > 0` there is a real polynomial `p` with

```
dist h (Polynomial.aeval g p) < ε.
```

This is `single_feature_polynomial_approx`. Here `dist` is the supremum (uniform) distance on
`C(X, ℝ)`, so the conclusion is a genuine uniform-approximation statement.

**EML exponential specialization.** Let `a b : ℝ` and consider the compact interval subtype
`{x : ℝ // x ∈ Set.Icc a b}`. Define the exponential feature

```
expFeature a b : C({x : ℝ // x ∈ Set.Icc a b}, ℝ),    expFeature a b x = Real.exp x.1.
```

Then for every continuous `h` on `[a, b]` and every `ε > 0` there is a real polynomial `p` with

```
dist h (Polynomial.aeval (expFeature a b) p) < ε.
```

This is `exp_polynomial_universal_on_Icc`.

## Why injective single-feature algebras separate points

The subalgebra generated by a single feature `g` is `Algebra.adjoin ℝ {g}`. To apply
Stone–Weierstrass we need this subalgebra to *separate points*: for any two distinct points
`x ≠ y` there must be a member of the subalgebra taking different values at `x` and `y`.

The generator `g` is itself a member of the subalgebra (`g ∈ Algebra.adjoin ℝ {g}`), so it is the
only witness we ever need. If `g` is injective, then `x ≠ y` immediately gives `g x ≠ g y`, because
`g x = g y` would force `x = y` by injectivity. Hence `g` separates `x` from `y`, and a single
injective feature suffices to separate all points. This is the content of
`adjoin_singleton_separatesPoints`. Note that injectivity is not only sufficient but morally
necessary: if `g` failed to be injective, every polynomial in `g` would collapse the two identified
points to a common value, so no function in the closure could separate them.

## The Stone–Weierstrass step

Stone–Weierstrass (real form, `ContinuousMap.subalgebra_topologicalClosure_eq_top_of_separatesPoints`)
states that a point-separating subalgebra of `C(X, ℝ)` on a compact space has topological closure
equal to the whole space `⊤`. Combined with the separation result above, the subalgebra generated by
an injective feature is therefore *dense* in `C(X, ℝ)` for the uniform norm
(`adjoin_singleton_closure_eq_top`).

Density is exactly the statement that every continuous function lies within `ε` of some member of
the subalgebra, for every `ε > 0`. Extracting such an `ε`-close member is the bridge to an explicit
witness.

## Identifying `p(exp x)` with exponential polynomials

The final ingredient is the algebraic description of a singly generated subalgebra. Mathlib's
`Algebra.adjoin_singleton_eq_range_aeval` identifies

```
Algebra.adjoin ℝ {g} = (Polynomial.aeval g).range,
```

that is, the subalgebra generated by `g` is precisely the set of values `Polynomial.aeval g p` as
`p` ranges over real polynomials. So the dense member produced by Stone–Weierstrass can be written
as `Polynomial.aeval g p` for an explicit polynomial `p`. This turns the abstract density statement
into the concrete polynomial witness of `single_feature_polynomial_approx`.

For the exponential feature, `Polynomial.aeval (expFeature a b) p` is the continuous function
`x ↦ p(exp x)`. Writing `p(t) = Σ c_n t^n`, this is `x ↦ Σ c_n (exp x)^n = Σ c_n exp(n x)`: a finite
linear combination of the exponentials `exp(n x)`. These are exactly the *exponential polynomials*
in the variable `exp x`. The theorem `exp_polynomial_universal_on_Icc` thus says: on any compact
interval, finite linear combinations of `exp(n x)` are uniformly dense in the continuous functions.
Injectivity of `exp` (used through `Real.exp_injective` and subtype extensionality in
`expFeature_injective`) is what licenses the single-feature argument, and the compactness of `[a, b]`
(through `isCompact_Icc`) supplies the `CompactSpace` instance Stone–Weierstrass requires.

## What is *not* proved here: a quantitative open problem

The result above is purely *qualitative*: it guarantees the existence of an approximating
exponential polynomial `p`, but says nothing about how complicated `p` must be. In particular it does
not control the degree of `p`, the magnitude of its coefficients, or any complexity measure of the
target function `h`.

A natural quantitative refinement would bound the resources needed for a given accuracy in terms of
the *Kolmogorov complexity* `K(h)` of the target. One could conjecture a bound of the rough shape
"degree (or description length) of an `ε`-approximating exponential polynomial is `O(K(h)/ε)`", or
some other explicit modulus relating accuracy, complexity, and polynomial size. **No such bound is
established here.** Proving (or refuting) any quantitative `K(h)`-dependent estimate requires
additional definitions (a fixed complexity model, an effective modulus of continuity, quantitative
Jackson/Bernstein-type approximation machinery) that are deliberately outside the scope of this
file. We record the quantitative bound only as an **open problem**, not as a theorem.

import Mathlib

/-!
# The Pickover / Clifford strange-attractor family: phase-space geometry

The **Clifford attractor** (a Pickover-type strange attractor) is the discrete
dynamical system on `ℝ²` generated by iterating the map

  `clifford a b c d (x, y) = (sin (a y) + c cos (a x), sin (b x) + d cos (b y))`.

For "interesting" parameter values its orbits accumulate on a fractal strange
attractor; the parameters `a, b, c, d` form the *bifurcation parameter space*
mentioned in the research brief.

This file establishes the **phase-space geometry** that holds for *every*
parameter value, independent of whether the long-term behaviour is chaotic:

* `clifford_fst_abs_le`, `clifford_snd_abs_le` — the explicit a-priori bounds
  `|x'| ≤ 1 + |c|`, `|y'| ≤ 1 + |d|` on a single step.
* `clifford_mapsTo_box` — *one step* sends the **whole plane** into the compact
  box `cliffordBox c d = [-(1+|c|), 1+|c|] × [-(1+|d|), 1+|d|]`; i.e. the box is
  *absorbing* in a single iteration.
* `clifford_forward_invariant` — consequently the box is forward invariant, so
  it contains the attractor for *all* parameter values: the strange attractor,
  whatever its shape, lives inside this explicit rectangle.

It also proves the two reusable Lipschitz facts `lip_sin_mul` / `lip_cos_mul`
that downstream files (`CliffordContraction`, `DeJongAttractor`) use to analyse
the contracting (point-attractor) regime of the bifurcation diagram.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
* **Hypothesis.** Even though the Clifford map can be chaotic, its image is
  *unconditionally* bounded, because each coordinate is a sine plus a scaled
  cosine. Conjecture: a single step is contained in an explicit rectangle whose
  size depends only on `c, d`.
* **Experiment.** Bounded `|sin(ay) + c cos(ax)| ≤ |sin(ay)| + |c||cos(ax)| ≤
  1 + |c|` via `abs_add_le`, `Real.abs_sin_le_one`, `Real.abs_cos_le_one`. The
  bound is independent of `a, b` and of the input point — strictly stronger than
  mere forward invariance: the rectangle is absorbing in *one* step
  (`clifford_mapsTo_box` from `Set.univ`).
* **Analysis.** Forward invariance (`clifford_forward_invariant`) is then a free
  corollary. This pins down where the attractor can live, uniformly over the
  bifurcation parameters; chaos is confined, never escaping to infinity.
* **Critique.** The bound `1 + |c|` is sharp: at `a = 0` the first coordinate is
  exactly `c cos 0 = c` plus `sin(0) = 0`... more precisely `|x'|` attains values
  arbitrarily close to `1 + |c|`, so the box cannot be shrunk in general.
* **Synthesis.** The geometry splits cleanly from the dynamics: boundedness is
  parameter-uniform, while the *type* of attractor (point vs. strange) is a
  parameter-dependent phenomenon studied in the companion files.
-/

open Real

noncomputable section

/-- The Clifford (Pickover-type) attractor map with parameters `a b c d`. -/
noncomputable def clifford (a b c d : ℝ) (p : ℝ × ℝ) : ℝ × ℝ :=
  (Real.sin (a * p.2) + c * Real.cos (a * p.1),
   Real.sin (b * p.1) + d * Real.cos (b * p.2))

/-! ## Reusable Lipschitz building blocks -/

/-- `t ↦ sin (a t)` is `|a|`-Lipschitz. -/
theorem lip_sin_mul (a : ℝ) :
    LipschitzWith (Real.nnabs a) (fun t : ℝ => Real.sin (a * t)) := by
  have ha : LipschitzWith (Real.nnabs a) (fun t : ℝ => a * t) := by
    rw [lipschitzWith_iff_norm_sub_le]; intro x y; rw [← mul_sub]
    simp [norm_mul, Real.norm_eq_abs, Real.coe_nnabs]
  simpa using Real.lipschitzWith_sin.comp ha

/-- `t ↦ cos (a t)` is `|a|`-Lipschitz. -/
theorem lip_cos_mul (a : ℝ) :
    LipschitzWith (Real.nnabs a) (fun t : ℝ => Real.cos (a * t)) := by
  have ha : LipschitzWith (Real.nnabs a) (fun t : ℝ => a * t) := by
    rw [lipschitzWith_iff_norm_sub_le]; intro x y; rw [← mul_sub]
    simp [norm_mul, Real.norm_eq_abs, Real.coe_nnabs]
  simpa using Real.lipschitzWith_cos.comp ha

/-- Multiplication by a constant `a` is `|a|`-Lipschitz on `ℝ`. -/
theorem lip_const_mul (a : ℝ) :
    LipschitzWith (Real.nnabs a) (fun t : ℝ => a * t) := by
  rw [lipschitzWith_iff_norm_sub_le]; intro x y; rw [← mul_sub]
  simp [norm_mul, Real.norm_eq_abs, Real.coe_nnabs]

/-! ## A-priori coordinate bounds -/

/-- A single Clifford step bounds the first coordinate by `1 + |c|`. -/
theorem clifford_fst_abs_le (a b c d : ℝ) (p : ℝ × ℝ) :
    |(clifford a b c d p).1| ≤ 1 + |c| := by
  have hsum : |(clifford a b c d p).1|
      ≤ |Real.sin (a * p.2)| + |c * Real.cos (a * p.1)| := by
    simpa [clifford] using abs_add_le (Real.sin (a * p.2)) (c * Real.cos (a * p.1))
  refine hsum.trans ?_
  have h1 : |Real.sin (a * p.2)| ≤ 1 := Real.abs_sin_le_one _
  have h2 : |c * Real.cos (a * p.1)| ≤ |c| := by
    rw [abs_mul]
    calc |c| * |Real.cos (a * p.1)| ≤ |c| * 1 :=
          mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left (Real.abs_cos_le_one _) (abs_nonneg _)
      _ = |c| := mul_one _
  linarith

/-- A single Clifford step bounds the second coordinate by `1 + |d|`. -/
theorem clifford_snd_abs_le (a b c d : ℝ) (p : ℝ × ℝ) :
    |(clifford a b c d p).2| ≤ 1 + |d| := by
  have hsum : |(clifford a b c d p).2|
      ≤ |Real.sin (b * p.1)| + |d * Real.cos (b * p.2)| := by
    simpa [clifford] using abs_add_le (Real.sin (b * p.1)) (d * Real.cos (b * p.2))
  refine hsum.trans ?_
  have h1 : |Real.sin (b * p.1)| ≤ 1 := Real.abs_sin_le_one _
  have h2 : |d * Real.cos (b * p.2)| ≤ |d| := by
    rw [abs_mul]
    calc |d| * |Real.cos (b * p.2)| ≤ |d| * 1 :=
          mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left (Real.abs_cos_le_one _) (abs_nonneg _)
      _ = |d| := mul_one _
  linarith

/-! ## The absorbing box -/

/-- The compact rectangle `[-(1+|c|), 1+|c|] × [-(1+|d|), 1+|d|]` that contains
the attractor for every parameter value. -/
def cliffordBox (c d : ℝ) : Set (ℝ × ℝ) :=
  Set.Icc (-(1 + |c|)) (1 + |c|) ×ˢ Set.Icc (-(1 + |d|)) (1 + |d|)

/-- One Clifford step maps the **entire plane** into `cliffordBox c d`: the box
is *absorbing* in a single iteration, uniformly over the parameters `a, b`. -/
theorem clifford_mapsTo_box (a b c d : ℝ) :
    Set.MapsTo (clifford a b c d) Set.univ (cliffordBox c d) := by
  intro p _
  exact ⟨abs_le.mp (clifford_fst_abs_le a b c d p),
         abs_le.mp (clifford_snd_abs_le a b c d p)⟩

/-- `cliffordBox c d` is forward invariant under the Clifford map: it contains
the attractor for every parameter value. -/
theorem clifford_forward_invariant (a b c d : ℝ) :
    Set.MapsTo (clifford a b c d) (cliffordBox c d) (cliffordBox c d) :=
  fun p _ => clifford_mapsTo_box a b c d (Set.mem_univ p)

end

import Mathlib

/-!
# Clifford attractor: the contracting (point-attractor) regime of the bifurcation diagram

Building on `Catalog.Novelty.CliffordAttractor` (the map `clifford` and the
reusable Lipschitz facts `lip_sin_mul` / `lip_cos_mul` / `lip_const_mul`), this
file analyses the *type* of attractor as a function of the bifurcation
parameters `a, b, c, d`.

The Clifford map is globally Lipschitz with explicit constant

  `cliffordK a b c d = max (|a|·(1+|c|)) (|b|·(1+|d|))`

in the sup metric on `ℝ²` (`clifford_lipschitz`). When `cliffordK < 1` the map
is a Banach contraction, so the **bifurcation diagram has a clean point-attractor
region**: there is a *unique* fixed point, *every* orbit converges to it
geometrically, and there is no strange attractor.

## Main results

* `clifford_lipschitz` — global Lipschitz constant `cliffordK`.
* `clifford_contractingWith` — contraction whenever `cliffordK < 1`.
* `clifford_exists_unique_fixedPoint` — unique fixed point in that regime.
* `clifford_tendsto_fixedPoint` — every orbit converges to the fixed point.
* `clifford_apriori_dist_le` — explicit geometric a-priori error bound.
* `clifford_pointAttractor_of_params_small` — a concrete sufficient condition
  `|a|·(1+|c|) < 1 ∧ |b|·(1+|d|) < 1` on the raw real parameters.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
* **Hypothesis.** The bifurcation diagram of attractor-type vs. parameter has a
  nonempty "point attractor" region near the origin of parameter space; there
  the strange attractor degenerates to a single globally attracting fixed point.
* **Experiment.** Computed the sup-norm Lipschitz constant component-by-component:
  `sin(a·)` and `cos(a·)` are `|a|`-Lipschitz (`lip_sin_mul`, `lip_cos_mul` from
  the catalog file), composition with the 1-Lipschitz projections
  (`LipschitzWith.prod_fst/​prod_snd`) and `LipschitzWith.add` give each
  coordinate constant `|a|(1+|c|)`, `|b|(1+|d|)`; `LipschitzWith.prodMk` then
  yields the `max`. Fed this to Mathlib's `ContractingWith` API.
* **Analysis.** "True but needs the right metric": the bound is natural in the
  **sup** (`Prod`) metric, not the Euclidean one — the `max` structure of the
  product metric matches the `max` of the two row sums exactly. With the
  Euclidean metric the constant would be messier.
* **Critique.** Is the result vacuous? No: e.g. `a=b=c=d=1/4` gives
  `cliffordK = 1/4·(5/4) = 5/16 < 1`, a genuine nonempty parameter region, so the
  point-attractor regime is real, not empty. The theorem is sharp in spirit:
  past `cliffordK = 1` the contraction argument necessarily fails, which is
  exactly where period-doubling / strange behaviour is observed numerically.
* **Synthesis.** Combined with the parameter-uniform absorbing box of the
  companion file, this gives a complete rigorous picture of one cell of the
  bifurcation diagram: bounded everywhere, single point attractor when
  `cliffordK < 1`.
-/

open Real

noncomputable section

/-! ## Component Lipschitz estimates -/

/-- The first coordinate of the Clifford map is `|a|·(1+|c|)`-Lipschitz. -/
theorem clifford_fst_lip (a b c d : ℝ) :
    LipschitzWith (Real.nnabs a * (1 + Real.nnabs c))
      (fun p : ℝ × ℝ => (clifford a b c d p).1) := by
  have h1 : LipschitzWith (Real.nnabs a) (fun p : ℝ × ℝ => Real.sin (a * p.2)) := by
    simpa using (lip_sin_mul a).comp (LipschitzWith.prod_snd (α := ℝ) (β := ℝ))
  have h2 : LipschitzWith (Real.nnabs c * Real.nnabs a)
      (fun p : ℝ × ℝ => c * Real.cos (a * p.1)) := by
    have hc : LipschitzWith (Real.nnabs a) (fun p : ℝ × ℝ => Real.cos (a * p.1)) := by
      simpa using (lip_cos_mul a).comp (LipschitzWith.prod_fst (α := ℝ) (β := ℝ))
    exact (lip_const_mul c).comp hc
  have hsum := h1.add h2
  have heq : Real.nnabs a + Real.nnabs c * Real.nnabs a
      = Real.nnabs a * (1 + Real.nnabs c) := by ring
  rw [heq] at hsum
  simpa [clifford] using hsum

/-- The second coordinate of the Clifford map is `|b|·(1+|d|)`-Lipschitz. -/
theorem clifford_snd_lip (a b c d : ℝ) :
    LipschitzWith (Real.nnabs b * (1 + Real.nnabs d))
      (fun p : ℝ × ℝ => (clifford a b c d p).2) := by
  have h1 : LipschitzWith (Real.nnabs b) (fun p : ℝ × ℝ => Real.sin (b * p.1)) := by
    simpa using (lip_sin_mul b).comp (LipschitzWith.prod_fst (α := ℝ) (β := ℝ))
  have h2 : LipschitzWith (Real.nnabs d * Real.nnabs b)
      (fun p : ℝ × ℝ => d * Real.cos (b * p.2)) := by
    have hc : LipschitzWith (Real.nnabs b) (fun p : ℝ × ℝ => Real.cos (b * p.2)) := by
      simpa using (lip_cos_mul b).comp (LipschitzWith.prod_snd (α := ℝ) (β := ℝ))
    exact (lip_const_mul d).comp hc
  have hsum := h1.add h2
  have heq : Real.nnabs b + Real.nnabs d * Real.nnabs b
      = Real.nnabs b * (1 + Real.nnabs d) := by ring
  rw [heq] at hsum
  simpa [clifford] using hsum

/-! ## Global Lipschitz constant and contraction -/

/-- The sup-metric Lipschitz constant of the Clifford map. -/
noncomputable def cliffordK (a b c d : ℝ) : NNReal :=
  max (Real.nnabs a * (1 + Real.nnabs c)) (Real.nnabs b * (1 + Real.nnabs d))

/-- The Clifford map is `cliffordK`-Lipschitz in the sup metric on `ℝ²`. -/
theorem clifford_lipschitz (a b c d : ℝ) :
    LipschitzWith (cliffordK a b c d) (clifford a b c d) := by
  have := (clifford_fst_lip a b c d).prodMk (clifford_snd_lip a b c d)
  simpa [clifford, cliffordK] using this

/-- When `cliffordK < 1`, the Clifford map is a Banach contraction. -/
theorem clifford_contractingWith (a b c d : ℝ) (hK : cliffordK a b c d < 1) :
    ContractingWith (cliffordK a b c d) (clifford a b c d) :=
  ⟨hK, clifford_lipschitz a b c d⟩

/-! ## Fixed-point structure and global convergence in the contracting regime -/

/-- In the contracting regime the Clifford map has a **unique** fixed point. -/
theorem clifford_exists_unique_fixedPoint (a b c d : ℝ) (hK : cliffordK a b c d < 1) :
    ∃! q : ℝ × ℝ, clifford a b c d q = q := by
  have hc := clifford_contractingWith a b c d hK
  exact ⟨ContractingWith.fixedPoint _ hc, hc.fixedPoint_isFixedPt,
    fun y hy => hc.fixedPoint_unique hy⟩

/-- In the contracting regime **every** orbit converges to the fixed point:
the attractor is a single point. -/
theorem clifford_tendsto_fixedPoint (a b c d : ℝ) (hK : cliffordK a b c d < 1)
    (x : ℝ × ℝ) :
    Filter.Tendsto (fun n => (clifford a b c d)^[n] x) Filter.atTop
      (nhds (ContractingWith.fixedPoint (clifford a b c d)
        (clifford_contractingWith a b c d hK))) :=
  (clifford_contractingWith a b c d hK).tendsto_iterate_fixedPoint x

/-- Explicit geometric a-priori error bound for the orbit of `x`. -/
theorem clifford_apriori_dist_le (a b c d : ℝ) (hK : cliffordK a b c d < 1)
    (x : ℝ × ℝ) (n : ℕ) :
    dist ((clifford a b c d)^[n] x)
        (ContractingWith.fixedPoint (clifford a b c d)
          (clifford_contractingWith a b c d hK))
      ≤ dist x (clifford a b c d x) * (cliffordK a b c d) ^ n
          / (1 - (cliffordK a b c d)) :=
  (clifford_contractingWith a b c d hK).apriori_dist_iterate_fixedPoint_le x n

/-- A concrete sufficient condition on the raw real parameters guaranteeing a
unique globally attracting fixed point (a "point attractor" cell of the
bifurcation diagram). -/
theorem clifford_pointAttractor_of_params_small (a b c d : ℝ)
    (ha : |a| * (1 + |c|) < 1) (hb : |b| * (1 + |d|) < 1) :
    ∃! q : ℝ × ℝ, clifford a b c d q = q := by
  apply clifford_exists_unique_fixedPoint
  have hca : (Real.nnabs a * (1 + Real.nnabs c) : NNReal) < 1 := by
    rw [← NNReal.coe_lt_coe]; push_cast [Real.coe_nnabs]; exact ha
  have hcb : (Real.nnabs b * (1 + Real.nnabs d) : NNReal) < 1 := by
    rw [← NNReal.coe_lt_coe]; push_cast [Real.coe_nnabs]; exact hb
  simpa [cliffordK, max_lt_iff] using ⟨hca, hcb⟩

end

  `deJong a b c d (x, y) = (sin (a y) - cos (b x), sin (c x) - cos (d y))`.

inhomogeneous additive structure (`sin - cos`) gives the uniform bound `2`.

  is an un-scaled trigonometric function of a single frequency: the relevant
  constant should be additive (`|a|+|b|`) rather than multiplicative.

/-- The Peter de Jong attractor map with parameters `a b c d`. -/
noncomputable def deJong (a b c d : ℝ) (p : ℝ × ℝ) : ℝ × ℝ :=
  (Real.sin (a * p.2) - Real.cos (b * p.1),
   Real.sin (c * p.1) - Real.cos (d * p.2))

/-! ## A-priori coordinate bounds -/

/-- A single de Jong step bounds the first coordinate by `2`. -/
theorem deJong_fst_abs_le (a b c d : ℝ) (p : ℝ × ℝ) :
    |(deJong a b c d p).1| ≤ 2 := by
  have hsum : |(deJong a b c d p).1|
      ≤ |Real.sin (a * p.2)| + |Real.cos (b * p.1)| := by
    simpa [deJong, sub_eq_add_neg] using
      abs_add_le (Real.sin (a * p.2)) (-Real.cos (b * p.1))
  have h1 := Real.abs_sin_le_one (a * p.2)
  have h2 := Real.abs_cos_le_one (b * p.1)
  linarith

/-- A single de Jong step bounds the second coordinate by `2`. -/
theorem deJong_snd_abs_le (a b c d : ℝ) (p : ℝ × ℝ) :
    |(deJong a b c d p).2| ≤ 2 := by
  have hsum : |(deJong a b c d p).2|
      ≤ |Real.sin (c * p.1)| + |Real.cos (d * p.2)| := by
    simpa [deJong, sub_eq_add_neg] using
      abs_add_le (Real.sin (c * p.1)) (-Real.cos (d * p.2))
  have h1 := Real.abs_sin_le_one (c * p.1)
  have h2 := Real.abs_cos_le_one (d * p.2)
  linarith

/-! ## The absorbing box -/

/-- The square `[-2, 2] × [-2, 2]` containing the de Jong attractor for every
parameter value. -/
def deJongBox : Set (ℝ × ℝ) :=
  Set.Icc (-2) 2 ×ˢ Set.Icc (-2) 2

/-- One de Jong step maps the entire plane into `deJongBox`: the box is absorbing
in a single iteration, uniformly over the parameters. -/
theorem deJong_mapsTo_box (a b c d : ℝ) :
    Set.MapsTo (deJong a b c d) Set.univ deJongBox := by
  intro p _
  refine ⟨abs_le.mp ?_, abs_le.mp ?_⟩
  · simpa using deJong_fst_abs_le a b c d p
  · simpa using deJong_snd_abs_le a b c d p

/-- `deJongBox` is forward invariant under the de Jong map. -/
theorem deJong_forward_invariant (a b c d : ℝ) :
    Set.MapsTo (deJong a b c d) deJongBox deJongBox :=
  fun p _ => deJong_mapsTo_box a b c d (Set.mem_univ p)

/-! ## Global Lipschitz constant and the point-attractor regime -/

/-- The first coordinate of the de Jong map is `(|a|+|b|)`-Lipschitz. -/
theorem deJong_fst_lip (a b c d : ℝ) :
    LipschitzWith (Real.nnabs a + Real.nnabs b)
      (fun p : ℝ × ℝ => (deJong a b c d p).1) := by
  have h1 : LipschitzWith (Real.nnabs a) (fun p : ℝ × ℝ => Real.sin (a * p.2)) := by
    simpa using (lip_sin_mul a).comp (LipschitzWith.prod_snd (α := ℝ) (β := ℝ))
  have h2 : LipschitzWith (Real.nnabs b) (fun p : ℝ × ℝ => Real.cos (b * p.1)) := by
    simpa using (lip_cos_mul b).comp (LipschitzWith.prod_fst (α := ℝ) (β := ℝ))
  simpa [deJong] using h1.sub h2

/-- The second coordinate of the de Jong map is `(|c|+|d|)`-Lipschitz. -/
theorem deJong_snd_lip (a b c d : ℝ) :
    LipschitzWith (Real.nnabs c + Real.nnabs d)
      (fun p : ℝ × ℝ => (deJong a b c d p).2) := by
  have h1 : LipschitzWith (Real.nnabs c) (fun p : ℝ × ℝ => Real.sin (c * p.1)) := by
    simpa using (lip_sin_mul c).comp (LipschitzWith.prod_fst (α := ℝ) (β := ℝ))
  have h2 : LipschitzWith (Real.nnabs d) (fun p : ℝ × ℝ => Real.cos (d * p.2)) := by
    simpa using (lip_cos_mul d).comp (LipschitzWith.prod_snd (α := ℝ) (β := ℝ))
  simpa [deJong] using h1.sub h2

/-- The sup-metric Lipschitz constant of the de Jong map. -/
noncomputable def deJongK (a b c d : ℝ) : NNReal :=
  max (Real.nnabs a + Real.nnabs b) (Real.nnabs c + Real.nnabs d)

/-- The de Jong map is `deJongK`-Lipschitz in the sup metric on `ℝ²`. -/
theorem deJong_lipschitz (a b c d : ℝ) :
    LipschitzWith (deJongK a b c d) (deJong a b c d) := by
  have := (deJong_fst_lip a b c d).prodMk (deJong_snd_lip a b c d)
  simpa [deJong, deJongK] using this

/-- When `deJongK < 1`, the de Jong map is a Banach contraction. -/
theorem deJong_contractingWith (a b c d : ℝ) (hK : deJongK a b c d < 1) :
    ContractingWith (deJongK a b c d) (deJong a b c d) :=
  ⟨hK, deJong_lipschitz a b c d⟩

/-- In the contracting regime the de Jong map has a unique fixed point. -/
theorem deJong_exists_unique_fixedPoint (a b c d : ℝ) (hK : deJongK a b c d < 1) :
    ∃! q : ℝ × ℝ, deJong a b c d q = q := by
  have hc := deJong_contractingWith a b c d hK
  exact ⟨ContractingWith.fixedPoint _ hc, hc.fixedPoint_isFixedPt,
    fun y hy => hc.fixedPoint_unique hy⟩

/-- In the contracting regime every de Jong orbit converges to the fixed point. -/
theorem deJong_tendsto_fixedPoint (a b c d : ℝ) (hK : deJongK a b c d < 1)
    (x : ℝ × ℝ) :
    Filter.Tendsto (fun n => (deJong a b c d)^[n] x) Filter.atTop
      (nhds (ContractingWith.fixedPoint (deJong a b c d)
        (deJong_contractingWith a b c d hK))) :=
  (deJong_contractingWith a b c d hK).tendsto_iterate_fixedPoint x

/-- A concrete sufficient condition on the raw real parameters guaranteeing a
unique globally attracting fixed point. -/
theorem deJong_pointAttractor_of_params_small (a b c d : ℝ)
    (hab : |a| + |b| < 1) (hcd : |c| + |d| < 1) :
    ∃! q : ℝ × ℝ, deJong a b c d q = q := by
  apply deJong_exists_unique_fixedPoint
  have h1 : (Real.nnabs a + Real.nnabs b : NNReal) < 1 := by
    rw [← NNReal.coe_lt_coe]; push_cast [Real.coe_nnabs]; exact hab
  have h2 : (Real.nnabs c + Real.nnabs d : NNReal) < 1 := by
    rw [← NNReal.coe_lt_coe]; push_cast [Real.coe_nnabs]; exact hcd
  simpa [deJongK, max_lt_iff] using ⟨h1, h2⟩

end

regardless of input and of `a,b`. Sampled numerically (rounded):

The bound is sharp: with `a=0`, `x' = sin(0)+c·cos(0) = c`, and perturbing the
frequency makes `|x'|` approach `1+|c|`. Hence the box cannot be uniformly shrunk.
This motivated the **one-step absorbing** theorem (`clifford_mapsTo_box` from
`Set.univ`), which is strictly stronger than plain forward invariance.

de Jong: `|sin - cos| ≤ 2`, so `[-2,2]²` is absorbing for all parameters.

Sup-metric Lipschitz constant computed:

* Clifford: `K = max(|a|(1+|c|), |b|(1+|d|))`.
* de Jong:  `K = max(|a|+|b|, |c|+|d|)`.

  in the absorbing box.

- **The key insight is** that contraction forces the ω-limit set to be the unique

    (hbound : 2 * Real.sqrt n ≤ α * q)
    (hγ : γ = n / α) :

    (hn : 1 ≤ n) (h1 : 0 < α₁) (h12 : α₁ ≤ α₂) :

/-!

This module formalizes the *worst-case* side of the Learning-with-Errors

LWE is at least as hard as solving the worst-case lattice problems **GapSVP**
and **SIVP** to within polynomial approximation factors.  Here we build the
concrete geometric foundation:

* a self-contained Euclidean length on integer vectors,
* the fact that the shortest nonzero vector of ℤⁿ has length exactly `1`
  (`integerLattice_min_attained` + `integerLattice_min_lower`),
* the **GapSVP promise** predicate and its gap-monotonicity reduction
  (`gapSVP_gap_monotone`): the problem only gets *easier* as the
  approximation factor grows,

  (`scaled_min_lower`, `scaled_min_attained`).

**Hypothesis (Hypothesizer).**
H1. Every nonzero point of ℤⁿ has Euclidean length ≥ 1, with equality attained.
H2. (surprising) GapSVP_γ becomes *easier*, not harder, as the approximation
    factor γ increases — a valid NO instance for a larger gap is automatically
    a valid NO instance for a smaller gap.
H3. Dilating a lattice by c > 0 scales its minimum distance by exactly c.

H1: reduced to "a nonzero integer has square ≥ 1" + `Finset.single_le_sum`.
H2: reduced to a linear inequality `g₁·d ≤ g₂·d` under `0 ≤ d`.
H3: factored through H1 by pulling the scalar c out of the length.

the promise algebra flips (verified in ComputationalEvidence.md) — "needs a
guard", not "false".

`n = 0` corner makes the minimum vacuous, so existence lemmas assume `0 < n`.

`by_contra`/`rcases`, or `linarith`.
-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--

* C. Peikert, "Public-Key Cryptosystems from the Worst-Case SVP", STOC 2009.

namespace LWEWorstCase

/-! ## Section 1: Euclidean length of integer vectors -/

/-- Squared Euclidean length of an integer vector, as a real number. -/
def sumSq {n : ℕ} (v : Fin n → ℤ) : ℝ := ∑ i, ((v i : ℝ)) ^ 2

/-- Euclidean length of an integer vector. -/
def latLen {n : ℕ} (v : Fin n → ℤ) : ℝ := Real.sqrt (sumSq v)

/-
The squared length is nonnegative.
-/
theorem sumSq_nonneg {n : ℕ} (v : Fin n → ℤ) : 0 ≤ sumSq v := by
  exact Finset.sum_nonneg fun _ _ => sq_nonneg _

/-
**Minimum distance lower bound.** Any nonzero integer vector has squared
length at least `1`: at least one coordinate is a nonzero integer, whose square
is `≥ 1`.
-/
theorem int_sumSq_ge_one {n : ℕ} (v : Fin n → ℤ) (hv : v ≠ 0) :
    (1 : ℝ) ≤ sumSq v := by
  obtain ⟨ i, hi ⟩ := Function.ne_iff.mp hv;
  exact le_trans ( by norm_cast; nlinarith [ mul_self_pos.mpr hi ] ) ( Finset.single_le_sum ( fun i _ => sq_nonneg ( v i : ℝ ) ) ( Finset.mem_univ i ) )

/-
**Minimum distance lower bound (length form).** Every nonzero point of the
integer lattice ℤⁿ has Euclidean length at least `1`.
-/
theorem integerLattice_min_lower {n : ℕ} (v : Fin n → ℤ) (hv : v ≠ 0) :
    1 ≤ latLen v := by
  exact Real.le_sqrt_of_sq_le ( by simpa using int_sumSq_ge_one v hv )

/-
**Minimum distance is attained.** For `n ≥ 1` there is a nonzero lattice
point of ℤⁿ of length exactly `1` (a standard basis vector).
-/
theorem integerLattice_min_attained {n : ℕ} (hn : 0 < n) :
    ∃ v : Fin n → ℤ, v ≠ 0 ∧ latLen v = 1 := by
  refine' ⟨ fun i => if i = ⟨ 0, hn ⟩ then 1 else 0, _, _ ⟩ <;> norm_num [ Function.ne_iff, latLen ];
  unfold sumSq; aesop;

/-! ## Section 2: GapSVP promise problem and gap monotonicity -/

/-- **GapSVP promise.** With shortest-vector length `lam`, threshold `d` and
approximation factor `gamma`, an instance satisfies the promise iff it is a
YES instance (`lam ≤ d`) or a clear NO instance (`gamma * d < lam`).  The gap
`(d, gamma*d]` is the "don't care" region. -/
def GapSVPpromise (lam d gamma : ℝ) : Prop := lam ≤ d ∨ gamma * d < lam

/-
**GapSVP gap monotonicity (the reduction).** For `0 ≤ d` and `g₁ ≤ g₂`,
any instance satisfying the *larger*-gap promise also satisfies the
*smaller*-gap promise.  Consequently an algorithm solving GapSVP at factor `g₁`
also solves GapSVP at every factor `g₂ ≥ g₁`: the problem gets easier as the
approximation factor grows.
-/
theorem gapSVP_gap_monotone {lam d g1 g2 : ℝ} (hd : 0 ≤ d) (hg : g1 ≤ g2)
    (h : GapSVPpromise lam d g2) : GapSVPpromise lam d g1 := by
  cases h <;> [ left; right ] <;> nlinarith

/-
**Strict separation of YES and NO instances.** Under the GapSVP promise
with positive threshold and gap `> 1`, a YES instance and a NO instance are
genuinely distinguishable: their `lam` values differ.
-/
theorem gapSVP_yes_no_separated {lamY lamN d gamma : ℝ}
    (hd : 0 < d) (hg : 1 ≤ gamma)
    (hY : lamY ≤ d) (hN : gamma * d < lamN) : lamY < lamN := by
  nlinarith

/-! ## Section 3: Scaling of the minimum distance -/

/-
**Scaled lower bound.** Dilating ℤⁿ by `c ≥ 0` makes every nonzero point
have length at least `c`.
-/
theorem scaled_min_lower {n : ℕ} (c : ℝ) (hc : 0 ≤ c)
    (v : Fin n → ℤ) (hv : v ≠ 0) : c ≤ c * latLen v := by
  exact le_mul_of_one_le_right hc ( integerLattice_min_lower v hv )

/-
**Scaled minimum attained.** For `n ≥ 1` and `c ≥ 0`, the dilated lattice
`c · ℤⁿ` has a nonzero point of length exactly `c`, so its minimum distance is
exactly `c`.
-/
theorem scaled_min_attained {n : ℕ} (hn : 0 < n) (c : ℝ) :
    ∃ v : Fin n → ℤ, v ≠ 0 ∧ c * latLen v = c := by
  obtain ⟨ v, hv₁, hv₂ ⟩ := integerLattice_min_attained hn ; use v ; aesop

end LWEWorstCase

end

# Computational Evidence — LWE Worst-Case Hardness Reductions

This note records small-case computational checks performed before formalizing
the worst-case-to-average-case reduction parameters for Learning with Errors
(Regev 2005 / Peikert 2009).

## 1. Minimum distance of the integer lattice ℤⁿ

For the standard integer lattice ℤⁿ ⊂ ℝⁿ, the squared Euclidean length of a
nonzero integer vector is a sum of squares of integers, at least one of which
is ≥ 1. Small cases:

| vector            | ∑ vᵢ²  | ‖v‖    |
|-------------------|--------|--------|
| (1,0,0)           | 1      | 1      |
| (1,1,0)           | 2      | √2     |
| (2,0,0)           | 4      | 2      |
| (1,1,1)           | 3      | √3     |
| (-1,0,0)          | 1      | 1      |

Minimum over nonzero vectors is exactly **1**, attained by any ± standard basis
vector. This grounds λ₁(ℤⁿ) = 1.

## 2. GapSVP gap monotonicity

GapSVP_γ at threshold d declares YES if λ₁ ≤ d, NO if λ₁ > γ·d. For fixed
λ₁ = 5, d = 1:

| γ   | γ·d | NO needs λ₁ > γ·d | instance |
|-----|-----|-------------------|----------|
| 2   | 2   | λ₁ > 2  (5>2 ✓)   | NO       |
| 4   | 4   | λ₁ > 4  (5>4 ✓)   | NO       |
| 6   | 6   | λ₁ > 6  (5>6 ✗)   | gap-violated |

Observation: a valid NO instance for a *larger* γ is automatically a valid NO
instance for any *smaller* γ. Hence GapSVP_γ becomes EASIER as γ grows — a
correct but counter-intuitive fact verified here numerically and proved in
`WorstCaseLattice.lean`.

## 3. Regev parameter regime  αq ≥ 2√n  and  γ = n/α

Regev's theorem: decision-LWE_{n,q,α} is at least as hard as quantumly solving
GapSVP_γ / SIVP_γ with γ = Õ(n/α), under αq ≥ 2√n. Sample feasibility checks
of the derived bound γ ≤ q√n / 2:

| n   | q     | α (min = 2√n/q) | γ = n/α     | q√n/2   | γ ≤ q√n/2 |
|-----|-------|-----------------|-------------|---------|-----------|
| 4   | 16    | 0.25            | 16          | 16      | ✓ (eq)    |
| 9   | 64    | 0.09375         | 96          | 96      | ✓ (eq)    |
| 16  | 256   | 0.03125         | 512         | 512     | ✓ (eq)    |

At the boundary α = 2√n/q the bound is tight (equality); for larger α it is
strict. This confirms the algebraic identity γ = q√n/2 at the boundary and the
inequality γ ≤ q√n/2 in general, both formalized in `ReductionParameters.lean`.

- "λ₁(ℤⁿ) could be < 1": tested all vectors with entries in {-2..2} for n ≤ 3;
  no nonzero vector has length < 1. No counterexample.
- "GapSVP monotonicity might fail when d < 0": indeed if d < 0 the promise
  algebra flips; the formal theorem therefore carries the hypothesis 0 ≤ d.
  Boundary recorded as an explicit hypothesis.
- "γ ≤ q√n/2 might fail for n = 0": √0 = 0 makes αq ≥ 0 vacuous and γ = n/α = 0;
  the formal theorem assumes 1 ≤ n to stay in the meaningful regime.

case became an explicit hypothesis on the Lean statement.

* `σ` denotes `ArithmeticFunction.sigma 1`, the sum-of-divisors function from Mathlib.
* The research brief defines `IsPerfect n := σ n = 2 * n`.  Taken literally this would make
  `0` a perfect number (`σ 0 = 0 = 2 * 0`), which breaks every downstream characterization
  (e.g. `0` is even and would have to be a Mersenne power).  To stay faithful to the
  mathematical intent — and to match Mathlib's `Nat.Perfect`, which also requires positivity —
  we bundle `0 < n` into `IsPerfect`.
-/

open ArithmeticFunction
open scoped sigma

namespace Perfect

/-- The abundancy index `σ(n)/n` of a natural number, as a rational number. -/
noncomputable def abundancyIndex (n : ℕ) : ℚ := (σ 1 n : ℚ) / (n : ℚ)

/-- A perfect number: `σ(n) = 2n` and `n > 0`.  (The positivity hypothesis is added to the
brief's definition `σ n = 2 * n` to exclude the degenerate value `n = 0`.) -/
def IsPerfect (n : ℕ) : Prop := σ 1 n = 2 * n ∧ 0 < n

/-- `p` is a Mersenne-prime exponent: both `2^p - 1` and `p` are prime. -/
def IsMersennePrime (p : ℕ) : Prop := Prime (2 ^ p - 1) ∧ Prime p

/-
For positive `n`, our `IsPerfect` coincides with Mathlib's `Nat.Perfect`.
-/
theorem isPerfect_iff_perfect {n : ℕ} : IsPerfect n ↔ Nat.Perfect n := by
  simp [IsPerfect, Nat.Perfect];
  simp +decide [ ArithmeticFunction.sigma_one_apply, two_mul, Nat.sum_divisors_eq_sum_properDivisors_add_self ]

/-
A number is perfect iff its abundancy index is `2`.
-/
theorem abundancyIndex_eq_two_iff {n : ℕ} : abundancyIndex n = 2 ↔ IsPerfect n := by
  by_cases hn : n = 0;
  · simp +decide [ hn, abundancyIndex, IsPerfect ];
  · unfold abundancyIndex IsPerfect; norm_cast; simp +decide [ hn, mul_comm, div_eq_iff ] ;
    exact ⟨ fun h => ⟨ mod_cast h, Nat.pos_of_ne_zero hn ⟩, fun h => mod_cast h.1 ⟩

/-! ## Part 1: Abundancy index properties -/

/-
The abundancy index is multiplicative on coprime arguments.
-/
theorem abundancyIndex_mul {m n : ℕ} (h : Nat.gcd m n = 1) :
    abundancyIndex (m * n) = abundancyIndex m * abundancyIndex n := by
  by_cases hm : m = 0 <;> by_cases hn : n = 0 <;> simp_all +decide [ abundancyIndex ];
  rw [ div_mul_div_comm, div_eq_div_iff ] <;> norm_cast <;> simp_all +decide [ ];
  convert ArithmeticFunction.isMultiplicative_sigma.map_mul_of_coprime h using 1

-/

    abundancyIndex (p ^ k) = ((p : ℚ) ^ (k + 1) - 1) / ((p : ℚ) ^ k * ((p : ℚ) - 1)) := by
  unfold abundancyIndex;
  simp_all +decide [ ← Nat.prime_iff, ArithmeticFunction.sigma ];
  rw [ geom_sum_eq ( mod_cast hp.ne_one ), div_div, mul_comm ]

  rw [ show n.Deficient ↔ ∑ d ∈ n.divisors, d < 2 * n from ?_ ];
  · rw [ abundancyIndex, div_lt_iff₀ ] <;> norm_cast;
    rw [ ArithmeticFunction.sigma_one_apply ];
  · rw [ Nat.sum_divisors_eq_sum_properDivisors_add_self, Nat.two_mul ];
    rw [ add_comm ] ; aesop

A number is abundant iff its abundancy index is `> 2`.

  by_cases hn : n = 0 <;> simp_all +decide [ Nat.Abundant ];
  rw [ lt_div_iff₀ ] <;> norm_cast;
  · simp +decide [ two_mul, ArithmeticFunction.sigma ];

import Mathlib
import Tropical.Core.TropicalSemiringProperties

/-!
# Order/Shift foundations for tropical differential equations

This file provides a *small, non-circular* foundation for tropical differential
equations.  An earlier attempted development of a "fundamental theorem of tropical
differential algebra" was circular: its main theorem ultimately relied on lemmas
that, in turn, depended on the theorem itself.  Rather than repairing that tangle,
this file restarts from elementary foundations and proves **only** support/order-level
facts together with a max/min algebra bridge.

Design constraints (deliberately respected here):

* This file does **not** import `Computation.TropicalDiffEq.FundamentalTheorem`, and it
  uses **no** theorem from that previous attempt.
* Every theorem below is proved from first principles (elementary `Nat` arithmetic) or
  from already-established catalog/Mathlib lemmas.  Nothing is self-referential: no
  theorem invokes itself directly or indirectly.
* We make no claim to prove the full tropical fundamental theorem of differential
  algebra.  This is strictly a foundation that later files may import.

## What we model

We model the *coefficient valuations* of a power series (or differential power series)
as a sequence `v : ℕ → WithTop ℕ`.  The intended interpretation is:

* `v n = ⊤`  means the `n`-th coefficient is **zero / absent**;
* `v n = (k : ℕ)` (a finite value) means the `n`-th coefficient is **nonzero**, with
  valuation `k`.

The *leading index* is the first index carrying a nonzero coefficient.  The *tropical
derivative* is the plain left shift `v ↦ (n ↦ v (n+1))`.  This deliberately ignores the
scalar factor `n+1` that a genuine derivative would multiply in: at the purely tropical
(support/order) level, multiplying a coefficient by a nonzero scalar does not change
whether it is zero, so the support and the leading index shift down by exactly one.
(A later, optional refinement could track the valuation of `n+1` as well; that belongs
in a separate lemma, not in the order-level statements here.)
-/

namespace Computation.TropicalDiffEq.OrderShift

/-- A coefficient-valuation sequence: `v n = ⊤` encodes a zero/absent coefficient,
while a finite `v n = k` encodes a nonzero coefficient of valuation `k`. -/
abbrev ValSeq := ℕ → WithTop ℕ

/-- `LeadingIndex v N` says that index `N` carries the *first* nonzero (finite)
coefficient of `v`: the coefficient at `N` is finite, and every earlier coefficient is
`⊤` (zero/absent). -/
def LeadingIndex (v : ValSeq) (N : ℕ) : Prop :=
  v N ≠ ⊤ ∧ ∀ n, n < N → v n = ⊤

/-- The tropical derivative on valuation sequences is the left shift.  It ignores the
coefficient factor `n+1`, capturing only the support/order behaviour. -/
def tropDeriv (v : ValSeq) : ValSeq := fun n => v (n + 1)

@[simp] theorem tropDeriv_apply (v : ValSeq) (n : ℕ) : tropDeriv v n = v (n + 1) := rfl

/-- **Main one-step theorem.**  Differentiating shifts the leading index down by one:
if `N > 0` is the leading index of `v`, then `N - 1` is the leading index of
`tropDeriv v`.

The proof uses only elementary `Nat` arithmetic: `(N - 1) + 1 = N` when `0 < N`, and
`m < N - 1 → m + 1 < N`.

(The name is kept *outside* the `LeadingIndex` namespace on purpose, so that the
identifier `tropDeriv` continues to refer to the shift operation inside the iterated
corollary below rather than to this theorem.) -/
theorem leadingIndex_tropDeriv {v : ValSeq} {N : ℕ} (hN : 0 < N)
    (h : LeadingIndex v N) : LeadingIndex (tropDeriv v) (N - 1) := by
  obtain ⟨htop, hzero⟩ := h
  refine ⟨?_, ?_⟩
  · -- `tropDeriv v (N-1) = v ((N-1)+1) = v N ≠ ⊤`.
    have hrw : (N - 1) + 1 = N := Nat.succ_pred_eq_of_pos hN
    simpa [tropDeriv, hrw] using htop
  · -- For `m < N - 1` we have `m + 1 < N`, hence `tropDeriv v m = v (m+1) = ⊤`.
    intro m hm
    have : m + 1 < N := by omega
    simpa [tropDeriv] using hzero (m + 1) this

/-- **Iterated version (corollary).**  Applying the tropical derivative `k` times shifts
the leading index down by `k`, as long as `k ≤ N`.  Proved by induction on `k` using the
one-step theorem `leadingIndex_tropDeriv`. -/
theorem leadingIndex_iterate_tropDeriv {v : ValSeq} {N : ℕ} :
    ∀ k, k ≤ N → LeadingIndex v N → LeadingIndex (tropDeriv^[k] v) (N - k)
  | 0, _, h => by simpa using h
  | k + 1, hk, h => by
    -- First take `k` derivatives, landing at leading index `N - k`.
    have hk' : k ≤ N := Nat.le_of_succ_le hk
    have ih : LeadingIndex (tropDeriv^[k] v) (N - k) :=
      leadingIndex_iterate_tropDeriv k hk' h
    -- One more derivative, using `0 < N - k` since `k + 1 ≤ N`.
    have hpos : 0 < N - k := by omega
    have step : LeadingIndex (tropDeriv (tropDeriv^[k] v)) (N - k - 1) :=
      leadingIndex_tropDeriv hpos ih
    -- Reconcile `tropDeriv ∘ tropDeriv^[k] = tropDeriv^[k+1]` and `N - k - 1 = N - (k+1)`.
    have hcomp : tropDeriv (tropDeriv^[k] v) = tropDeriv^[k + 1] v := by
      rw [Function.iterate_succ_apply']
    have hidx : N - k - 1 = N - (k + 1) := by omega
    rw [hcomp, hidx] at step
    exact step

/-!
## Min-plus algebra bridge (independent of the derivative theorems)

Tropical differential equations are usually phrased over the **min-plus** semiring
`(ℝ, min, +)` (valuations add, and the order/leading behaviour is governed by `min`).
The catalog file `Tropical.Core.TropicalSemiringProperties` instead develops the
**max-plus** semiring `(ℝ, max, +)`.  The two are conjugate via negation.

Below we record the min-plus right-distributivity law `min a b + c = min (a+c) (b+c)`,
derived by conjugating the catalog's max-plus law
`TropicalSemiringProperties.tropical_scalar_distrib_right` through negation.  This bridge
is completely independent of the derivative/order theorems above. -/

/-- **Min-plus right distributivity.**  Derived by conjugating the catalog max-plus law
`TropicalSemiringProperties.tropical_scalar_distrib_right` through negation
(`-max (-x) (-y) = min x y`). -/
theorem minplus_scalar_distrib_right (a b c : ℝ) :
    min a b + c = min (a + c) (b + c) := by
  -- Conjugate the max-plus statement at `-a, -b, -c` through negation.
  have hmax := TropicalSemiringProperties.tropical_scalar_distrib_right (-a) (-b) (-c)
  -- `hmax : max (-a) (-b) + (-c) = max (-a + -c) (-b + -c)`.
  have hl : min a b + c = -(max (-a) (-b) + -c) := by
    rw [neg_add, neg_neg, ← min_neg_neg, neg_neg, neg_neg]
  have hr : -(max (-a + -c) (-b + -c)) = min (a + c) (b + c) := by
    have e1 : (-a + -c) = -(a + c) := by ring
    have e2 : (-b + -c) = -(b + c) := by ring
    rw [e1, e2, ← min_neg_neg, neg_neg, neg_neg]
  rw [hl, hmax, hr]

/-- Direct/standalone proof of the same min-plus law, for convenience (does not depend on
the catalog file).  Kept alongside `minplus_scalar_distrib_right` so downstream files can
use whichever they prefer. -/
theorem minplus_scalar_distrib_right' (a b c : ℝ) :
    min a b + c = min (a + c) (b + c) := by
  rcases le_total a b with h | h <;>
    simp_all

end Computation.TropicalDiffEq.OrderShift

# Orderly Friedman numbers (OEIS A080035)

A *Friedman number* is a positive integer that can be written, in a nontrivial
way, as an expression using its own digits (each digit used exactly once, in any
order) together with the operations `+`, `*`, exponentiation, unary minus and
parentheses.  An *orderly* Friedman number (OEIS A080035) is a Friedman number
admitting such an expression in which the digits appear in their natural reading
order (most-significant first).

This file formalizes orderly Friedman numbers.  We model digit expressions by an
inductive type `FExpr` over a small set of binary operations `FOp`
(`add`, `mul`, `pow`), with unary negation and single-digit literals.  We define
`eval` (the integer value of an expression), `digitSeq` (the left-to-right
sequence of digit literals) and `numLits` (the number of digit literals).

The predicate `IsOrderlyFriedman n` asks for an expression with at least two
digit literals whose digit sequence equals the digits of `n` in reading order
(`(Nat.digits 10 n).reverse`) and which evaluates to `n`.  The predicate
`IsFriedman n` only requires the digit sequence to be a permutation of the digits
of `n`.

Main results:
* five explicit witnesses (`127`, `343`, `736`, `1285`, `2592`);
* `numLits_eq_length`: `numLits e = (digitSeq e).length`;
* `orderlyFriedman_ge_ten`: orderly Friedman numbers have at least two digits;
* `no_two_digit_orderlyFriedman`: there are no two-digit orderly Friedman numbers;
* `orderly_imp_friedman`: every orderly Friedman number is a Friedman number;
* `digits_in_order`: the defining expression has its digits in reading order.
-/
import Mathlib

namespace OrderlyFriedman

/-- The binary operations allowed in digit expressions. -/
inductive FOp
  | add
  | mul
  | pow
  deriving DecidableEq, Repr

/-- Digit expressions: single-digit literals, unary negation and binary
operations. -/
inductive FExpr
  | lit (d : Nat)
  | neg (e : FExpr)
  | bin (op : FOp) (l r : FExpr)
  deriving Repr

/-- Apply a binary operation to two integers.  Exponentiation uses the
natural-number truncation of the exponent. -/
def FOp.apply : FOp → Int → Int → Int
  | FOp.add, a, b => a + b
  | FOp.mul, a, b => a * b
  | FOp.pow, a, b => a ^ b.toNat

/-- The integer value of a digit expression. -/
def eval : FExpr → Int
  | FExpr.lit d => (d : Int)
  | FExpr.neg e => - eval e
  | FExpr.bin op l r => op.apply (eval l) (eval r)

/-- The left-to-right sequence of digit literals occurring in an expression. -/
def digitSeq : FExpr → List Nat
  | FExpr.lit d => [d]
  | FExpr.neg e => digitSeq e
  | FExpr.bin _ l r => digitSeq l ++ digitSeq r

/-- The number of digit literals in an expression. -/
def numLits : FExpr → Nat
  | FExpr.lit _ => 1
  | FExpr.neg e => numLits e
  | FExpr.bin _ l r => numLits l + numLits r

/-- `n` is an *orderly Friedman number*: it can be written using its own digits,
in reading order, with at least two digit literals. -/
def IsOrderlyFriedman (n : Nat) : Prop :=
  ∃ e : FExpr, numLits e ≥ 2 ∧ digitSeq e = (Nat.digits 10 n).reverse ∧ eval e = (n : Int)

/-- `n` is a *Friedman number*: it can be written using its own digits, in any
order, with at least two digit literals. -/
def IsFriedman (n : Nat) : Prop :=
  ∃ e : FExpr, numLits e ≥ 2 ∧ (digitSeq e).Perm (Nat.digits 10 n) ∧ eval e = (n : Int)

/-- `127 = -1 + 2^7`. -/

  ⟨FExpr.bin FOp.add (FExpr.neg (FExpr.lit 1))
      (FExpr.bin FOp.pow (FExpr.lit 2) (FExpr.lit 7)), by native_decide⟩

/-- `343 = (3 + 4)^3`. -/

/-- `736 = 7 + 3^6`. -/

(The informal description `1 * 2^8 + 5` does not evaluate to `1285`; the correct
reading-order expression is `(1 + 2^8) * 5 = 257 * 5 = 1285`.) -/
theorem orderlyFriedman_1285 : IsOrderlyFriedman 1285 :=
  ⟨FExpr.bin FOp.mul

/-- `2592 = 2^5 * 9^2`. -/
theorem orderlyFriedman_2592 : IsOrderlyFriedman 2592 :=
  ⟨FExpr.bin FOp.mul (FExpr.bin FOp.pow (FExpr.lit 2) (FExpr.lit 5))

/-! ## Structural lemmas -/

/-- The number of digit literals equals the length of the digit sequence. -/
theorem numLits_eq_length (e : FExpr) : numLits e = (digitSeq e).length := by
  induction e with
  | lit d => rfl
  | neg e ih => simpa [numLits, digitSeq] using ih
  | bin op l r ihl ihr => simp [numLits, digitSeq, ihl, ihr]

/-- Every expression has at least one digit literal. -/
theorem numLits_pos (e : FExpr) : 1 ≤ numLits e := by
  induction e with
  | lit d => simp [numLits]
  | neg e ih => simpa [numLits] using ih
  | bin op l r ihl ihr => simp [numLits]; omega

/-- An expression with a single digit literal evaluates to plus or minus that
digit. -/
theorem single_leaf (e : FExpr) (h1 : numLits e = 1) :
    ∃ d : Nat, digitSeq e = [d] ∧ (eval e = (d : Int) ∨ eval e = -(d : Int)) := by
  induction e with
  | lit d => exact ⟨d, rfl, Or.inl rfl⟩
  | neg e ih =>
      obtain ⟨d, hd, hv⟩ := ih (by simpa [numLits] using h1)
      refine ⟨d, by simpa [digitSeq] using hd, ?_⟩
      rcases hv with hv | hv
      · exact Or.inr (by simp [eval, hv])
      · exact Or.inl (by simp [eval, hv])
  | bin op l r ihl ihr =>
      exfalso
      have hl := numLits_pos l
      have hr := numLits_pos r
      simp [numLits] at h1
      omega

/-- A value `v` is *reachable* from two digits `a`, `b` (in this order) if it can
be obtained by combining `±a` and `±b` with one operation and an outer sign. -/
def reachable2 (a b : Nat) (v : Int) : Prop :=
  ∃ s0 s1 s2 : Bool,
      v = (if s0 then -1 else 1) *
            ((if s1 then -(a : Int) else (a : Int)) + (if s2 then -(b : Int) else (b : Int)))
    ∨ v = (if s0 then -1 else 1) *

    ∨ v = (if s0 then -1 else 1) *

theorem reachable2_of (a b : Nat) (x y : Int) (op : FOp)

# Orderly Friedman numbers (OEIS A080035)

A *Friedman number* is a positive integer that can be written, in a nontrivial
way, as an expression using its own digits (each digit used exactly once, in any
order) together with the operations `+`, `*`, exponentiation, unary minus and
parentheses.  An *orderly* Friedman number (OEIS A080035) is a Friedman number
admitting such an expression in which the digits appear in their natural reading
order (most-significant first).

This file formalizes orderly Friedman numbers.  We model digit expressions by an
inductive type `FExpr` over a small set of binary operations `FOp`
(`add`, `mul`, `pow`), with unary negation and single-digit literals.  We define
`eval` (the integer value of an expression), `digitSeq` (the left-to-right
sequence of digit literals) and `numLits` (the number of digit literals).

The predicate `IsOrderlyFriedman n` asks for an expression with at least two
digit literals whose digit sequence equals the digits of `n` in reading order
(`(Nat.digits 10 n).reverse`) and which evaluates to `n`.  The predicate
`IsFriedman n` only requires the digit sequence to be a permutation of the digits
of `n`.

Main results:
* five explicit witnesses (`127`, `343`, `736`, `1285`, `2592`);
* `numLits_eq_length`: `numLits e = (digitSeq e).length`;
* `orderlyFriedman_ge_ten`: orderly Friedman numbers have at least two digits;
* `no_two_digit_orderlyFriedman`: there are no two-digit orderly Friedman numbers;
* `orderly_imp_friedman`: every orderly Friedman number is a Friedman number;
* `digits_in_order`: the defining expression has its digits in reading order.
-/
import Mathlib

namespace OrderlyFriedman

/-- The binary operations allowed in digit expressions. -/
inductive FOp
  | add
  | mul
  | pow
  deriving DecidableEq, Repr

/-- Digit expressions: single-digit literals, unary negation and binary
operations. -/
inductive FExpr
  | lit (d : Nat)
  | neg (e : FExpr)
  | bin (op : FOp) (l r : FExpr)
  deriving Repr

/-- Apply a binary operation to two integers.  Exponentiation uses the
natural-number truncation of the exponent. -/
def FOp.apply : FOp → Int → Int → Int
  | FOp.add, a, b => a + b
  | FOp.mul, a, b => a * b
  | FOp.pow, a, b => a ^ b.toNat

/-- The integer value of a digit expression. -/
def eval : FExpr → Int
  | FExpr.lit d => (d : Int)
  | FExpr.neg e => - eval e
  | FExpr.bin op l r => op.apply (eval l) (eval r)

/-- The left-to-right sequence of digit literals occurring in an expression. -/
def digitSeq : FExpr → List Nat
  | FExpr.lit d => [d]
  | FExpr.neg e => digitSeq e
  | FExpr.bin _ l r => digitSeq l ++ digitSeq r

/-- The number of digit literals in an expression. -/
def numLits : FExpr → Nat
  | FExpr.lit _ => 1
  | FExpr.neg e => numLits e
  | FExpr.bin _ l r => numLits l + numLits r

/-- `n` is an *orderly Friedman number*: it can be written using its own digits,
in reading order, with at least two digit literals. -/
def IsOrderlyFriedman (n : Nat) : Prop :=
  ∃ e : FExpr, numLits e ≥ 2 ∧ digitSeq e = (Nat.digits 10 n).reverse ∧ eval e = (n : Int)

/-- `n` is a *Friedman number*: it can be written using its own digits, in any
order, with at least two digit literals. -/
def IsFriedman (n : Nat) : Prop :=
  ∃ e : FExpr, numLits e ≥ 2 ∧ (digitSeq e).Perm (Nat.digits 10 n) ∧ eval e = (n : Int)

theorem single_leaf (e : FExpr) (h1 : numLits e = 1) :
    ∃ d : Nat, digitSeq e = [d] ∧ (eval e = (d : Int) ∨ eval e = -(d : Int)) := by

      · exact Or.inr (by simp [eval, hv])

def reachable2 (a b : Nat) (v : Int) : Prop :=

theorem reachable2_of (a b : Nat) (x y : Int) (op : FOp)

  obtain ⟨s2, hy⟩ : ∃ s2 : Bool, y = if s2 then -(b : Int) else (b : Int) := by

  · exact Or.inr (Or.inl (by simp [FOp.apply]))
  · exact Or.inr (Or.inr (by simp [FOp.apply]))

theorem reachable2_neg (a b : Nat) (v : Int) (h : reachable2 a b v) :

  obtain ⟨s0, s1, s2, h⟩ := h

  · exact Or.inr (Or.inl (by rw [h, hsgn]; ring))
  · exact Or.inr (Or.inr (by rw [h, hsgn]; ring))

theorem eval_numLits_two (e : FExpr) (a b : Nat) (h2 : numLits e = 2)

# The Fitting no-revival law for endomorphism powers

For a linear endomorphism `g : V →ₗ[K] V` on a finite-dimensional `K`-vector space
`V`, the sequence `k ↦ finrank K (range (g ^ k))` is antitone and eventually
constant.  The *Fitting no-revival law* strengthens this: the very first index `k`
at which the sequence fails to strictly decrease is already the index at which it
has reached its final, stable value.  In other words there is no
"plateau-then-drop" behaviour — once the rank of a power stops dropping it never
drops again.

This file builds the result in five steps:

* `range_pow_succ_le` : the ranges of successive powers are nested.
* `range_pow_succ_eq_of_finrank_eq` : equal finranks of successive ranges force the
  ranges themselves to be equal.
* `range_pow_stable` : once two successive ranges agree, every later range agrees
  with them.
* `rank_pow_plateau_implies_stable` : the finrank version of stability.
* `rank_pow_strictAnti_until_stable` : the dichotomy expressing the no-revival law.
-/
import Mathlib

namespace Catalog.Algebra.TransEndoFitting

open LinearMap Module Submodule

variable {K V : Type*} [Field K] [AddCommGroup V] [Module K V] [FiniteDimensional K V]

/-- The range of `g ^ (n + 1)` is contained in the range of `g ^ n`, since
`g ^ (n + 1) = g ^ n ∘ₗ g` and the image of a composition through `g ^ n` lies in
the range of `g ^ n`. -/
omit [FiniteDimensional K V] in
theorem range_pow_succ_le (g : V →ₗ[K] V) (n : ℕ) :
    range (g ^ (n + 1)) ≤ range (g ^ n) := by
  rw [pow_succ]
  show range ((g ^ n) ∘ₗ g) ≤ range (g ^ n)
  rw [LinearMap.range_comp]
  exact LinearMap.map_le_range

/-- If the ranges of `g ^ (k + 1)` and `g ^ k` have the same finrank, then they are
equal as submodules. -/
theorem range_pow_succ_eq_of_finrank_eq (g : V →ₗ[K] V) (k : ℕ)
    (h : finrank K (range (g ^ (k + 1))) = finrank K (range (g ^ k))) :
    range (g ^ (k + 1)) = range (g ^ k) :=
  Submodule.eq_of_le_of_finrank_eq (range_pow_succ_le g k) h

/-- Once two successive ranges agree (`range (g ^ (k + 1)) = range (g ^ k)`), every
later power has the same range. -/
omit [FiniteDimensional K V] in
theorem range_pow_stable (g : V →ₗ[K] V) {k : ℕ}
    (h : range (g ^ (k + 1)) = range (g ^ k)) (m : ℕ) (hm : k ≤ m) :
    range (g ^ m) = range (g ^ k) := by
  obtain ⟨j, rfl⟩ := Nat.exists_eq_add_of_le hm
  induction j with
  | zero => simp
  | succ n ih =>
    have key : g ^ (k + (n + 1)) = (g ^ n) ∘ₗ (g ^ (k + 1)) := by
      show g ^ (k + (n + 1)) = (g ^ n) * (g ^ (k + 1))
      rw [← pow_add]; congr 1; omega
    rw [key, LinearMap.range_comp, h, ← LinearMap.range_comp]
    show range ((g ^ n) * (g ^ k)) = range (g ^ k)
    rw [← pow_add]
    have hnk : n + k = k + n := by omega
    rw [hnk]
    exact ih (by omega)

/-- The finrank version of stability: if the finranks of `range (g ^ (k + 1))` and
`range (g ^ k)` agree, then every later power has the same finrank. -/
theorem rank_pow_plateau_implies_stable (g : V →ₗ[K] V) {k : ℕ}
    (h : finrank K (range (g ^ (k + 1))) = finrank K (range (g ^ k)))
    (m : ℕ) (hm : k ≤ m) :
    finrank K (range (g ^ m)) = finrank K (range (g ^ k)) := by
  rw [range_pow_stable g (range_pow_succ_eq_of_finrank_eq g k h) m hm]

/-- The Fitting no-revival law: at every index `k`, either the rank strictly
decreases from `k` to `k + 1`, or the rank has already stabilised at index `k`
(it equals the rank of every later power). -/
theorem rank_pow_strictAnti_until_stable (g : V →ₗ[K] V) (k : ℕ) :
    finrank K (range (g ^ (k + 1))) < finrank K (range (g ^ k)) ∨
      (∀ m ≥ k, finrank K (range (g ^ m)) = finrank K (range (g ^ k))) := by
  have hle : finrank K (range (g ^ (k + 1))) ≤ finrank K (range (g ^ k)) :=
    Submodule.finrank_mono (range_pow_succ_le g k)
  rcases lt_or_eq_of_le hle with hlt | heq
  · exact Or.inl hlt
  · exact Or.inr (fun m hm => rank_pow_plateau_implies_stable g heq m hm)

end Catalog.Algebra.TransEndoFitting

# Computational Evidence

Evidence supporting the two theorems proved this cycle. All rank computations below
are over a field `K` with `V` the standard finite-dimensional coordinate space; they
were used to choose the witnesses before formalization.

## 1. Single-endomorphism rank profile is strictly-decreasing-then-flat

Take the nilpotent Jordan block `J` of size `d` (ones on the super-diagonal). The
ranks of its powers are:

| n           | 0 | 1   | 2   | … | d-1 | d | d+1 | … |
|-------------|---|-----|-----|---|-----|---|-----|---|
| rank(Jⁿ)    | d | d-1 | d-2 | … | 1   | 0 | 0   | … |

The profile decreases by exactly `1` at each step until it hits `0`, then is flat —
matching `rank_pow_strictAnti_until_stable` and `range_pow_stable`. The diagonalizable
extreme `g = 1` gives the all-flat profile `d, d, d, …` (always the "stable" branch).
These two extremes confirm both disjuncts of the dichotomy are realized.

## 2. The stream counterexample (the 2D witness)

Stream maps over `K²`:

* `A = projA = [[1,0],[0,0]]`  (rank 1),
* `f 1 = id`,
* `B = projB = [[0,0],[0,1]]`  (rank 1).

Composite ranks of `compFrom f 0 n` (the product `f(n-1) ∘ ⋯ ∘ f 0`):

| n                | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 |
|------------------|---|---|---|---|
| map              | id| A | id∘A = A | B∘A |
| `B·A` (matrix)   |   |   |   | `[[0,0],[0,1]]·[[1,0],[0,0]] = 0` |
| rank             | 2 | 1 | 1 | 0 |

So the rank sequence is `2, 1, 1, 0`: a genuine **plateau** at `1` across the step
`1 → 2`, followed by a **strict drop** to `0` at `2 → 3`. This is exactly
`stream_rank_plateau_then_drop`, and it is impossible for a single endomorphism by
Section 1.

## 3. Counterexample hunt / robustness

* Replacing `f 1 = id` by any invertible map keeps `rk₁ = rk₂` and the drop persists,
  so the phenomenon is not an artifact of the identity.
* Making the stream *constant* (`f ≡ A`) collapses the composites to powers `Aⁿ`
  (this is `compFrom_const`), and the profile becomes `2, 1, 1, 1, …` — flat after the
  first drop, i.e. the rigidity returns. This is the computational seed for
  Conjecture 3 in `FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.md`.

No counterexample to the *single-endomorphism* rigidity was found in a sweep of random
`2×2`–`4×4` rational matrices (ranks of powers were always strictly-decreasing-then-flat),
consistent with the proved theorem.

# Future Directions — Transition-rank rigidity of endomorphism streams

This cycle continued the `Catalog.Algebra.TransEndo` line. The catalog already had:

* `TransEndo` — the iterated-composition / transition operator `compFrom`, `transEndo`,
  and the *soft* fact that its rank is antitone;
* `TransEndoStabilization` — the transition-rank sequence is bounded, antitone, and
  therefore **eventually constant** (no rate).

New this cycle (both files fully proved, `sorry`-free, only `propext/Classical.choice/Quot.sound`):

* `TransEndoFitting` — a **hard** stabilization law for a *single* endomorphism:
  the rank of `gⁿ` strictly decreases until its final value, then is flat forever
  (`rank_pow_strictAnti_until_stable`); a single non-strict step freezes the range
  permanently (`range_pow_stable`).
* `TransEndoStreamPlateau` — an explicit `2`-dimensional **counterexample** showing
  that this rigidity *fails* for non-constant streams: a stream whose transition rank
  plateaus (`rk₁ = rk₂`) and then strictly drops (`rk₃ < rk₂`). The bridge
  `compFrom_const` pins the difference on constancy/commutativity.

The contrast (rigid for one endomorphism, flexible for a stream) drives the following
falsifiable conjectures.

---

## Conjecture 1 — Rate bound: the stabilization index is at most `finrank K V`

For a single `g : Module.End K V` over a finite-dimensional `V`, the least `N` with
`finrank (range (gᴺ⁺¹)) = finrank (range (gᴺ))` satisfies `N ≤ finrank K V`, and for
all `m ≥ N` the rank is constant.

The key insight is that `rank_pow_strictAnti_until_stable` makes every pre-stabilization
step a *strict* drop of a natural number bounded below by `0` and above by `finrank K V`;
a strictly decreasing finite chain of naturals cannot be longer than its starting value,
so the index is bounded by the dimension. **Why now?** The dichotomy lemma proved this
cycle converts "eventually constant" into "strictly decreasing then flat," which is
exactly the structure a counting argument needs — the soft `TransEndoStabilization`
result could not supply a rate.

## Conjecture 2 — Fitting decomposition at the plateau

At the stabilization index `N` of a single endomorphism, `V = ker (gᴺ) ⊕ range (gᴺ)`,
with `g` nilpotent on the first summand and an isomorphism on the second.

The key insight is that `range_pow_stable` already shows the range chain freezes at `N`;
dualizing the same one-step argument to the *ascending* kernel chain
`ker (gⁿ) ≤ ker (gⁿ⁺¹)` should freeze it at the *same* index, and equal-index
saturation of both chains is precisely Fitting's lemma. **Why now?** We have the range
half in hand as a reusable lemma; only the (formally dual) kernel half and the
complementation step remain, so the decomposition is one structural induction away.

## Conjecture 3 — Commutativity restores rigidity for streams

If every map in a stream commutes (`∀ a b, f a ∘ₗ f b = f b ∘ₗ f a`), then the
transition-rank sequence `m ↦ rk (compFrom f 0 m)` is again strictly decreasing until
its final value and flat thereafter — i.e. the single-endomorphism rigidity returns.

The key insight is that the `TransEndoStreamPlateau` counterexample is built from two
*non-commuting* projections (`projA`, `projB`), and the only place the single-endomorphism
proof used constancy was to turn `compFrom` into a power via `compFrom_const`; commutativity
is the weaker hypothesis that should still let `range (compFrom)` be pushed forward
coherently. **Why now?** The counterexample isolates non-commutativity as the precise
lever, so commutativity is the natural minimal hypothesis to test next.

## Conjecture 4 — Descent budget for arbitrary streams

For *any* stream over a finite-dimensional `V`, the number of strictly-decreasing steps
in `m ↦ rk (compFrom f 0 m)` is at most `finrank K V`, even though individual plateaus
between drops can be arbitrarily long.

The key insight is that the rank is a bounded antitone `ℕ → ℕ` sequence, so its total
descent (start minus eventual value) is `≤ finrank K V`; the counterexample shows
plateaus and drops can interleave, but the *count* of drops is still dimension-bounded.
**Why now?** This cycle produced both the antitone bound (catalog) and an explicit
interleaving plateau/drop pattern, making the "long plateaus but few drops" picture
concrete and ready to quantify.
